short: The idea that people who come together acquire new characteristics and become open to suggestion and contagion; made famous by Le Bon (1895), later criticised by social-identity approaches.
body:
Crowd psychology says that people who come together acquire characteristics they do not have one by one. Le Bon (1895) names three causes: a feeling of invincible power together with anonymity, contagion and, most important, suggestibility. The result is that the person descends several rungs on the ladder of civilisation. [[cite:le-bon-1895-psychologie-foules]] In his account this is added to the inherited traits tied to a people’s “race”. [[cite:encyclopedia-le-bon-european-social-history]]

Crowd psychology arose at the end of the nineteenth century first among judges and writers who dealt with crime and criminality; Reicher argues that it was an “establishment response”. The same author writes that in the Bristol 1980 data crowd behaviour was targeted and limited, and that this is explained by a shared social identity; on this view the limit of contagion is the limit of shared identity. [[cite:reicher-1984-st-pauls-riot]]

Today the term does two different jobs: a historical current, Le Bon’s theory of the crowd, and the effort in social psychology to explain crowd behaviour; the two should not be confused.
example: (Hypothetical example.) If at a rally a proposal that nobody alone would approve is accepted without objection, Le Bon would explain it by suggestion and contagion; Reicher would look at shared identity.
